items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Natural capital that can be generated or replaced as fast as it is used, e.g. living species, forests, fish stocks, solar energy"?
items.answer: renewable natural capital
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of renewable natural capital.

items.stem: Distinguish between non-renewable natural capital and renewable natural capital.
items.answer: Renewable natural capital regenerates on human timescales if used within its yield (forests, fish); non-renewable capital forms over geological time and is depleted by use (oil, copper).
items.markingKey: Renewable natural capital regenerates on human timescales if used within its yield (forests, fish); non-renewable capital forms over geological time and is depleted by use (oil, copper). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Outline why some renewable resources are being depleted.
items.answer: They are harvested faster than they regenerate (overfishing, deforestation); habitat damage reduces regeneration; open access encourages over-use (tragedy of the commons).

items.answer: Renewable resources are only sustainable if harvested within their natural income; poorly managed renewables can collapse, as Atlantic cod did.

items.answer: If extraction exceeds the replacement rate - e.g. pumping fossil groundwater faster than recharge, eroding soil faster than it forms - the stock is depleted and may take centuries or millennia to recover.

items.stem: Suggest why lithium is described as a critical raw material.
items.answer: It is essential for batteries in EVs and grid storage, demand is rising rapidly, supply is concentrated (Australia, Chile, China), and extraction has environmental and social impacts (water use in the Atacama).
items.markingKey: It is essential for batteries in EVs and grid storage, demand is rising rapidly, supply is concentrated (Australia, Chile, China), and extraction has environmental and social impacts (water use in the Atacama).

items.stem: With reference to whaling and whale-watching, explain in detail the causes and consequences involved in the changing value of resources. [7]
items.answer: Commercial whaling for oil peaked in the 20th century; the 1986 IWC moratorium followed, and whale-watching now attracts about 13 million people a year. Technological substitutes and changing values transformed whales from an extractive to a non-consumptive resource. A second, contrasting example should be developed in the same way.

items.stem: Outline how the Törbel community in Switzerland has managed alpine pasture sustainably for centuries.
items.answer: Rules dating from 1483 limit the number of cows each household can graze to the number it can feed over winter; monitoring and fines enforce the rules - an example used by Ostrom.
items.markingKey: Rules dating from 1483 limit the number of cows each household can graze to the number it can feed over winter; monitoring and fines enforce the rules - an example used by Ostrom.

items.stem: Outline one argument for and one argument against the view that renewable resources will always be more sustainable than non-renewable resources.
items.answer: Renewable resources are only sustainable if harvested within their natural income; poorly managed renewables can collapse, as Atlantic cod did.
items.markingKey: For: they regenerate within human timescales. Against: renewable stocks such as fisheries, forests and aquifers can be overexploited beyond recovery. items.stem: Using the case study and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that community management is more effective than government regulation for sustaining natural resources.
items.answer: Community management works well for local commons, but large-scale resources require government and international regulation; co-management combines the strengths of both.

items.stem: Explain, with named examples, the differences between renewable, replenishable and non-renewable natural capital and how each can be managed sustainably. [7]
items.answer: Definitions; examples (forests, fish; groundwater, soil, ozone; fossil fuels, minerals); sustainable management (harvest within yield, recharge-based limits, recycling and substitution).
items.markingKey: Indicative content: Definitions; examples (forests, fish; groundwater, soil, ozone; fossil fuels, minerals); sustainable management (harvest within yield, recharge-based limits, recycling and substitution). items.stem: Which of the following best describes "common-pool resource"?
options: The use of resources at a rate that does not exceed their regeneration and that maintains ecosystems and benefits for future generations
A resource that is shared, where one person's use reduces availability to others and it is difficult to exclude users, e.g. fisheries or grazing land
Keeping materials in use through reuse, repair and recycling, reducing extraction of new resources
The value of a resource that can be expressed in market prices
items.answer: A resource that is shared, where one person's use reduces availability to others and it is difficult to exclude users, e.g. fisheries or grazing land
items.markingKey: B. "common-pool resource" is a resource that is shared, where one person's use reduces availability to others and it is difficult to exclude users, e.g. fisheries or grazing land.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "non-renewable natural capital".
items.answer: Natural capital that is either irreplaceable or replaced only over geological timescales, e.g. fossil fuels, minerals

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The sum of use values (direct, indirect, option) and non-use values (existence, bequest) of a resource"?
items.answer: total economic value

items.stem: Outline why certification schemes can help achieve sustainable resource use.
items.answer: They set independent standards, allow consumers and businesses to choose sustainably produced goods, and reward producers with market access or premium prices; but they rely on trust, audits and consumer demand.
items.markingKey: They set independent standards, allow consumers and businesses to choose sustainably produced goods, and reward producers with market access or premium prices; but they rely on trust, audits and consumer demand. [1] per valid point, up to [3].

items.stem: Briefly explain why reserves of non-renewable resources can increase over time.
items.answer: Higher prices make lower-grade deposits economic; new technology (fracking, deep-sea drilling) allows extraction of previously inaccessible deposits; exploration discovers new deposits.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher prices make lower-grade deposits economic; new technology (fracking, deep-sea drilling) allows extraction of previously inaccessible deposits; exploration discovers new deposits. items.stem: Explain the difference between intrinsic value and economic value.
items.answer: Economic value reflects usefulness to people and can often be priced; intrinsic value is value in itself, independent of human use, central to ecocentric worldviews.
items.markingKey: Economic value reflects usefulness to people and can often be priced; intrinsic value is value in itself, independent of human use, central to ecocentric worldviews. items.stem: Isabel writes: "The tragedy of the commons proves that only privatisation can protect shared resources." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Ostrom showed many communities manage commons sustainably through local institutions; privatisation or state control are not the only solutions.
items.markingKey: Ostrom showed many communities manage commons sustainably through local institutions; privatisation or state control are not the only solutions. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Renewable resources can be used without limit." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Living renewable resources are limited by their regeneration rate; exceeding it depletes the stock.
items.markingKey: Living renewable resources are limited by their regeneration rate; exceeding it depletes the stock. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "A resource's value is fixed by its physical properties." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Value depends on human needs, technology, culture and markets, which change over time.
items.markingKey: Value depends on human needs, technology, culture and markets, which change over time. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.answer: Handing control to local users gave them incentives and rules to protect and regenerate forests.

items.stem: Proven reserves of world natural gas are 180.0 trillion m³; production is 3.6 trillion m³ per year. (a) Calculate the static R/P ratio. (b) If production grows by 3% per year, the reserves last n years where n = ln(1 + g·R/P)/ln(1 + g) (g as a decimal). Calculate n. (c) Explain why R/P ratios are poor predictors of when a resource will run out.
items.answer: (a) ≈ 50 years (b) n = ln(1 + 0.03 × 50) / ln(1.03) ≈ 31 years (c) reserves change with prices, technology and new discoveries (dynamic nature of resources); demand changes with substitution and policy (e.g. phasing out coal); recycling extends supply; some reserves become uneconomic.
items.markingKey: (a) A1 50. (b) M1 substitution, A1 ≈ 31. (c) R1 R1 dynamic reserves / demand changes.
